title: The Ethos of Fenumion
dek: How to inhabit Fenumion: remember its people, make choices, and leave something behind.

body:
Fenumion is not a campaign built around one party, one plot, or a queue of adventures waiting to be completed. It is a world. Your character enters it, lives in it, changes it, is changed by it, and eventually becomes part of its history.

Important events may begin as quests, but they also begin as tavern conversations, arguments, mistakes, kindnesses, forgotten objects, failed investigations, discoveries, and choices whose importance is understood only much later.

This is not a list of rules. It explains the assumptions beneath Fenumion: what kind of world you are entering, what freedom you have inside it, and how to get the most from playing here.

01

The world comes first

Fenumion does not come into existence when your party arrives. Places have histories before you discover them. People have relationships when you are absent. Factions possess goals that are not quests for you, and dangers are not necessarily placed where they are level-appropriate.

Treat Fenumion as a place rather than an adventure interface. Return later. Ignore something. Follow a detail nobody expected you to care about. Ask questions beyond the apparent objective. The essential question is often not What are we supposed to do? but What would my character actually do if this were real?

02

You have agency, not narrative supremacy

Your choices matter enormously. The world is not required to make those choices succeed. You may save a life, found an institution, create an enemy, start a war, or leave a consequence inherited by people you never meet. You may also fail, arrive too late, misunderstand someone, or lose what mattered.

None of that removes agency. Agency means your choices are real enough for the world to answer them honestly. It does not guarantee your preferred outcome. There is no single protagonist of Fenumion; your character can become tremendously important without the world becoming theirs.

03

The past remains true

Fenumion remembers. A destroyed building remains destroyed until someone rebuilds it. Promises, reputations, roads, schools, graves, friendships, feuds, gardens, and forgotten objects can matter years later because people kept interacting with them.

Continuity is not merely remembered lore; it is preserved causality. A later discovery may change what an old event means without changing what happened. Old knowledge, relationships, and mistakes remain useful. The world has a memory, and your character is allowed to have one too.

04

Knowledge is incomplete

NPCs, books, religions, governments, scholars, eyewitnesses, enemies, friends, and powerful beings can all be wrong or incomplete. Two honest people may contradict one another because they understand the same event differently. A successful check reveals what that check could reasonably uncover; it does not create omniscience.

You may form a theory without knowing whether it is true, miss something, or carry an answer without recognizing it. Fenumion rewards curiosity, memory, experimentation, comparison, and better questions. Do not be afraid to be wrong. Being wrong in an interesting way is often where discovery begins.

05

Fiction comes before the check

Do not search your character sheet for the button that solves the scene. Describe what your character is attempting: examine where a fire began, invoke a promise someone remembers, or watch a geyser field for the pattern observed last time.

Mechanics, abilities, spells, and statistics still matter. They adjudicate what your character is doing in the world; they do not replace it. The clearer the intention and method, the more honestly the world can answer.

06

The environment is real

Terrain is not decoration. Weather, distance, materials, visibility, buildings, roads, water, elevation, vegetation, fire, ruins, fortifications, infrastructure, and previous damage can all matter. Preparation matters too.

Learn how the world behaves. Change terrain before a fight. Use a storm, test a material, or prepare for a dangerous journey. Listed mechanics cover common interactions, not everything the fiction permits. Creative ideas are welcome because the fiction is mechanically relevant; the world will still answer each attempt honestly.

07

Power does not create permission

Power answers What can I do? It does not automatically answer What am I allowed to decide for everyone else? Resurrection, compulsion, imprisonment, destruction, authority, and overwhelming force do not create consent or moral ownership.

Ask Who gets to decide? and Who is being asked to pay the price? Choosing to sacrifice yourself is different from deciding someone else should be sacrificed. Responsibility, stewardship, and leadership matter, but caring for something does not mean owning it.

08

Other characters are people, not resources

This applies to PCs and NPCs. A person is not necessarily a quest giver, merchant, clue dispenser, obstacle, follower, rival, or future combatant. They have priorities, can say no, may misunderstand you, and can remember kindness or cruelty.

Fenumion is strongest when characters help make each other interesting instead of competing for narrative control. Listen, react, allow surprise, and leave room for choices you would not make. Everyone can leave a mark on the world. Nobody owns it.

09

Failure is history too

Failure is not a loading screen. A lost battle can change a government. A failed rescue can create grief, guilt, revenge, reconciliation, or an absence someone else eventually fills. Retreat can preserve lives that matter later, and misunderstandings can endure until someone compares the right evidence.

Even resurrection does not erase death. People experienced it, places may have changed, relationships may have broken, and someone may return to a world that continued without them. Consequences are not punishment for playing incorrectly. They are evidence that what you did was real.

10

Ordinary things matter

Fenumion contains gods, wars, ancient powers, impossible magic, and world-ending dangers. It also contains meals, taverns, gardens, schools, funerals, markets, homes, jobs, tired people, children, and people who remember their town before the adventurers arrived.

These are not filler between important scenes. They are why the important scenes matter. Saving the world means little if nothing in it is worth saving. Rebuilding a home may leave as real a mark as killing a legendary monster. History is not measured only in challenge rating.

11

Creativity is welcome; entitlement is not

Try strange things. Use spells unexpectedly, talk to enemies, avoid fights, build, research, combine old information, recruit help, retreat, negotiate, lie, tell a costly truth, or follow the side path. Fenumion should permit approaches nobody planned.

Creative does not mean guaranteed success. An idea may work brilliantly, work partly, fail for a discoverable reason, or succeed and create an unforeseen problem. The DM’s role is not to reward every idea with victory, but to let the world respond fairly.

12

There is no required story

You may walk away, investigate the wrong person, leave a mystery unsolved, solve an old mystery accidentally, care about the gravedigger more than the archmage, turn an incidental person into a lifelong friend, or make a choice nobody expected.

Fenumion’s strongest stories often emerge because the world existed, the characters made real choices, and everyone accepted what became true afterward. Do not worry too much about finding “the plot.” Live in the world. The plot will be whatever history says happened.

13

Hope matters because loss matters

Fenumion can be dangerous, melancholy, unfair, and full of things that cannot simply be undone. It is not cynical. People rebuild, remember, plant what they may never see mature, preserve knowledge for strangers, resurrect friends when they can, bury them when they cannot, and make homes where ruins stood.

Hope is not a promise that everything will work out as intended. It is the belief that what people build, protect, remember, and give one another is worth fighting for.

How to play Fenumion

If you remember nothing else

Treat the world as real.

Remember people, places, and what happened before. Ask questions. Make theories and accept that they may be wrong. Use your abilities creatively without confusing power with ownership. Let other characters choose. Allow failure to become history. Care about small things. Return to old things. Leave something behind.

Fenumion does not ask you to discover the story written for you. It asks you to live in a world carefully enough that, years later, everyone can look backward and realize that a story happened.

The world comes first. Your character enters it second. What happens after that belongs to everyone who was there.
